meanings.short: A group of hundreds to thousands of galaxies held together by their shared gravity: the largest bound objects in the universe.
meanings.long: Clusters weigh about 10¹⁴ to 10¹⁵ solar masses. Most of that is dark matter; most of the ordinary matter is hot gas between the galaxies, not stars. Fritz Zwicky first argued for dark matter from the speeds of galaxies in the Coma cluster in 1933.

meanings.short: The hot, thin gas, at tens of millions of degrees, that fills the space between the galaxies of a cluster.
meanings.long: It holds most of a cluster's ordinary matter, several times the mass in its stars. It shines in X-rays, and its temperature and density, assumed in hydrostatic equilibrium, weigh the cluster.

origin: German Bremsen, braking, and Strahlung, radiation.

meanings.short: Radiation given off by fast electrons as they are deflected, and so slowed or turned, by passing ions.
meanings.long: The name means braking radiation. The hot gas of galaxy clusters shines in X-rays this way; the brightness tells its density and the spectrum its temperature.

meanings.short: Light of very short wavelength, from about 0.01 to 10 nanometres, between ultraviolet light and gamma rays.
meanings.long: X-ray photons carry hundreds to tens of thousands of electronvolts. Gas at millions of degrees, such as in galaxy clusters or near black holes, shines in X-rays. Earth's atmosphere absorbs them, so X-ray telescopes are flown in space.

meanings.short: A pair of galaxy clusters seen just after colliding, whose mass, mapped by lensing, has separated from their hot gas.
meanings.long: The gas clouds collided and were slowed, while the galaxies and most of the mass passed through each other. The weak-lensing mass follows the galaxies, not the gas, which holds most of the ordinary matter: strong evidence for collisionless dark matter. Its catalogue name is 1E 0657−558.

meanings.short: A curved shock wave in front of an object moving faster than sound through a gas, like the wave at the bow of a boat.
meanings.long: In the Bullet Cluster the smaller cluster's gas shows one, the sign that it is moving faster than sound through the other cluster's gas. Gas crossing the shock is suddenly compressed and heated.

meanings.short: The spread of the random speeds of stars, galaxies or particles about their average, measured as the root mean square of the differences.
meanings.long: In a galaxy or cluster held up by random motions it plays the part of a temperature. With the system's size it gives its mass through the virial theorem; elliptical galaxies have velocity dispersions of about 200 to 300 km/s.

meanings.short: Of a galaxy, star cluster or galaxy cluster: held up against gravity by the random motions of its members, not by orderly rotation.
meanings.long: Its stars move in all directions, and their velocity dispersion acts like the pressure of a hot gas. Elliptical galaxies and globular clusters are mostly pressure-supported.

meanings.short: Of a galaxy: held up against gravity mainly by the orderly rotation of its stars and gas, as a spiral galaxy's disc is.
meanings.long: Its rotation speed at each radius, the rotation curve, then measures the mass inside that radius. Such systems are called cold, because their random motions are small compared with the rotation.

meanings.short: Like the orbits of planets around the Sun under Kepler's laws: with orbital speed falling as one over the square root of distance.
meanings.long: A Keplerian rotation curve is what one expects outside a central mass. Galaxies' rotation curves stay flat far out instead of falling in this Keplerian way, the classic evidence for dark matter.

meanings.short: A model of a galaxy or halo in which every part has the same velocity dispersion; its density falls as one over radius squared.
meanings.long: It gives a perfectly flat rotation curve. In its simplest, singular form the central density is infinite and the total mass grows without limit, so real models add a core or an outer cut-off.

meanings.short: An isothermal sphere given a flat central core, so its density stays finite at the centre and falls as one over radius squared far out.
meanings.long: Its density is ρ₀ divided by 1 + (r/r_c)². It fits the rotation curves of many dwarf and low surface brightness galaxies better than the cuspy NFW profile.

meanings.short: A cored density profile for dark matter halos, flat in the centre and falling as one over radius cubed far out, like NFW.
meanings.long: Andreas Burkert proposed it in 1995 to fit the rotation curves of dwarf galaxies, which seem to have cores rather than cusps. Like the pseudo-isothermal sphere it gives a rising rotation curve in the centre.

meanings.short: A density profile for dark matter halos whose slope steepens smoothly with radius, with one extra shape number α.
meanings.long: The logarithm of its density falls as a power of radius. With α about 0.2 it matches simulated halos even better than NFW; a cored version shifts the radius to make a flat centre.

meanings.short: A density profile, falling as one over radius at the centre and one over radius to the fourth far out, that fits elliptical galaxies' stars.
meanings.long: Lars Hernquist introduced it in 1990. Its potential and mass have simple closed forms, which makes it popular in models and simulations.

meanings.short: The rate at which the logarithm of one quantity changes with the logarithm of another: the local power in a power law.
meanings.long: For a density profile it is d ln ρ / d ln r. It is −2 for an isothermal sphere, −1 at the centre of an NFW halo and 0 in a core.

meanings.short: The radius in a profile's formula that sets its size, marking where the inner, shallower fall gives way to the steeper outer one.
meanings.long: For an NFW halo it is the radius r_S (written a in some books), where the logarithmic slope is −2. The halo's outer radius divided by its scale radius is its concentration.

meanings.short: The radius that contains half of a galaxy's light or mass.
meanings.long: It is the usual measure of a galaxy's size. Seen on the sky it is the projected effective radius. Half-light and half-mass radii differ slightly, and each can be measured in projection or in three dimensions.

meanings.short: The radius reached by matter falling into a halo at the far point of its first orbit, a natural outer edge of the halo.
meanings.long: Just inside it the density drops steeply. Unlike the virial radius it does not depend on an arbitrary density threshold.

meanings.short: A galaxy that has fallen through a cluster and come out the other side, so it is now found well outside the cluster.
meanings.long: It carries the marks of its passage, such as lost gas, even though it now looks like a field galaxy. Some galaxies counted as isolated may therefore once have been cluster members.

meanings.short: Shaped like a squashed and stretched ball with three different axis lengths, like a flattened rugby ball.
meanings.long: Dark matter halos are triaxial rather than spherical. The triaxiality, built from the axis ratios, says whether a halo is more like a rugby ball or more like a flattened disc.

meanings.short: A number λ that measures how fast a halo rotates compared with the rotation it would need to be held up by spin alone.
meanings.long: It combines angular momentum, energy and mass so that units cancel. Simulated halos have λ of only a few hundredths: they are held up almost entirely by random motions.

meanings.short: The large-scale pattern of matter in the universe: sheets and filaments of galaxies around huge empty voids, with clusters where filaments meet.
meanings.long: It grows by gravity from the early density ripples, as simulations of cold dark matter show. Halos sit along the filaments and at their nodes.

meanings.short: The dependence of how halos cluster on properties other than their mass, such as when they formed.
meanings.long: Halos of equal mass can have different formation histories and environments. Models that describe galaxies by halo mass alone miss this, so extended models add concentration, formation time or spin.

meanings.short: A smaller dark matter halo orbiting inside a larger one, left over after it fell in.
meanings.long: Being small, subhalos collapsed early and are dense, so they survive the tides of their host. Satellite galaxies live in subhalos; dark subhalos would hold no stars.

meanings.short: The smaller halos and clumps that survive inside a larger dark matter halo.
meanings.long: Cold dark matter predicts a lot of substructure, down to very small masses; warm dark matter would erase the smallest pieces. Lensing and the gaps it leaves in stellar streams may reveal substructure that holds no stars.

meanings.short: A small galaxy orbiting a larger one, inside its halo, such as the Magellanic Clouds around the Milky Way.
meanings.long: About fifty are known around the Milky Way and about thirty around Andromeda. In models of galaxies in halos, satellites fell in with their own halos, now subhalos.

meanings.short: The main galaxy of a dark matter halo, sitting at its centre, as opposed to the satellites orbiting around it.
meanings.long: Halo models treat centrals and satellites separately: a halo above some mass has one central and a number of satellites that grows with its mass. Centrals are usually the brightest galaxy in their halo.

meanings.short: A small, faint galaxy, below about a billion solar masses; the faintest, ultra-faint dwarfs, have under about 100,000 solar masses of stars.
meanings.long: Dwarf galaxies are dominated by dark matter, which makes them good tests of its nature. Most known dwarfs are satellites of the Milky Way or Andromeda.

meanings.short: A galaxy whose stars are spread so thinly that, per area of sky, it is fainter than the glow of the night sky itself.
meanings.long: Such galaxies are dominated by dark matter even in their centres, so their rotation curves test halo profiles directly; many favour cores. Because they are so faint, they were long missed by surveys.

meanings.short: An object's mass divided by its luminosity, usually in units of the Sun's; a high value means much mass gives little light.
meanings.long: Stars alone give values up to about 10 in visible light, depending on age, metallicity and the initial mass function. The outskirts of galaxies and galaxy clusters have tens to hundreds: evidence for dark matter.

meanings.short: A test that gives a galaxy's stars the largest mass the inner rotation curve allows, to see how much dark matter must remain.
meanings.long: Even with the stars as heavy as possible, the flat outer rotation curves of spirals still need a dark halo. Whether real discs are maximal is still debated.

meanings.short: A factor of ten, counted on a logarithmic scale: 1 dex is a factor of 10, 0.2 dex a factor of about 1.6.
meanings.long: Short for decimal exponent. Astronomers use it for uncertainties and ranges of quantities that span many powers of ten, such as stellar masses. A spread of 0.3 dex is a factor of about two either way.

meanings.short: The difficulty that an older stellar population and a more metal-rich one look alike: both are redder.
meanings.long: Colours and many spectral features cannot tell them apart, so stellar ages and masses carry large uncertainties. Dust adds a third look-alike: a red colour may mean old, metal-rich or dusty.

meanings.short: Of an initial mass function: with more massive stars than usual (top-heavy) or more low-mass stars than usual (bottom-heavy).
meanings.long: A bottom-heavy IMF adds mass but little light, raising the mass-to-light ratio; it is suggested in the cores of massive galaxies. A top-heavy one lowers it, as in strongly star-forming galaxies. The standard Salpeter or Chabrier forms are neither.

meanings.short: A graph of the colours of stars or galaxies against their brightness, which sorts them into groups.
meanings.long: For galaxies it shows two populations: the blue cloud of star-forming galaxies and the red sequence of galaxies that have stopped forming stars. For stars it picks out, for example, the members of a faint dwarf galaxy.

meanings.short: The group of galaxies on a colour–magnitude diagram that are still forming stars, so their light is blue; mostly spirals.
meanings.long: Galaxies move from the blue cloud to the red sequence when star formation stops, for example through feedback. Few galaxies sit between the blue cloud and the red sequence, so the change must be fairly quick.

meanings.short: The narrow band of red galaxies on a colour–magnitude diagram that have stopped forming stars; mostly ellipticals.
meanings.long: Their colours redden slightly with brightness because larger galaxies are more metal-rich. Most galaxies in rich clusters lie on it.

meanings.short: The trend that the most massive galaxies formed their stars earliest, with star formation shifting to smaller galaxies over time.
meanings.long: It seems to run against hierarchical growth, in which small halos form first. Feedback explains it: black holes stop star formation in large halos early, supernovae slow it in small ones.

meanings.short: Energy and momentum that stars, supernovae and black holes return to the gas around them, heating it or blowing it out and slowing star formation.
meanings.long: Supernova feedback matters most in small galaxies, whose shallow wells lose gas easily; feedback from active nuclei in large ones. Without it, simulations form far too many stars. Feedback that drives gas out of a halo's centre may also turn a cusp into a core.

meanings.short: The failure of early galaxy-formation models without feedback: gas cooled and formed stars too early and too fast.
meanings.long: They made too many old, massive, compact galaxies with too little rotation. Adding supernova and black-hole feedback solves it.

meanings.short: Growth of a galaxy from gas that is shock-heated to the halo's virial temperature as it falls in, then cools and sinks to the centre.
meanings.long: It dominates in massive halos. In small halos and at early times gas can instead flow in cold along filaments without being heated, called cold-mode accretion.

meanings.short: The growth of a halo by dark matter that was never part of a smaller halo, as opposed to growth by mergers.
meanings.long: Simulations suggest it supplies about 40 per cent of a halo's mass. The rest arrives through mergers with smaller halos.

meanings.short: Steady, spherical infall of gas onto a black hole or star, at a rate set by its mass and the gas's density and sound speed.
meanings.long: Hermann Bondi worked it out in 1952: the rate grows as the square of the mass and falls as the cube of the sound speed. Simulations use it, with a fudge factor and capped at the Eddington rate, to grow black holes.

meanings.short: The distance within which a body's gravity, such as a black hole's, outweighs that of the surrounding stars and gas.
meanings.long: It is roughly GM divided by the square of the gas sound speed or of the stars' velocity dispersion: about 50 parsecs for a ten-million-solar-mass black hole in gas with a sound speed of 30 km/s. That is still below the resolution of galaxy simulations, so black hole growth must be added as a recipe.

meanings.short: The growth of a galaxy and its central black hole together, each affecting the other.
meanings.long: The evidence is that black hole masses follow the velocity dispersions of their galaxies' bulges closely. Feedback from the black hole is thought to regulate star formation in the galaxy.

meanings.short: Processes too small for a simulation to follow directly, such as star formation and feedback, added through simple rules called recipes.
meanings.long: Their strengths are tuned to match observations such as the galaxy stellar mass function. Different recipes can give the same result, which is the main uncertainty of galaxy simulations.

meanings.short: The physics of flowing fluids such as gas: how pressure, gravity and motion change their density, speed and temperature.
meanings.long: In galaxy simulations the gas is followed with the fluid equations: continuity, Euler and energy equations. Gas, unlike dark matter, collides, so it feels pressure, shocks and cooling.

meanings.short: A computer calculation that follows many particles moving under their mutual gravity, step by step, to see how structure forms.
meanings.long: Each simulation particle stands for an enormous number of real dark matter particles. Today's runs follow billions of particles; the best reach a resolution of about 100 parsecs.

meanings.short: A small distance below which a simulation weakens the force between particles, to avoid huge forces at tiny separations.
meanings.long: The potential is changed to −Gm/√(r² + ε²), that of a Plummer sphere. The softening length ε sets the smallest scale the simulation can resolve, its force resolution.

meanings.short: A simple model of a ball of stars whose potential is minus GM over the square root of r² plus a core radius squared.
meanings.long: Henry Plummer used it in 1911 for globular clusters. Simulations use its form to soften the force between particles.

meanings.short: A fast way of computing gravity in a simulation by grouping distant particles into cells and treating each cell as one mass.
meanings.long: Summing every pair of particles costs about N² steps; a tree code, with distant cells opened only when needed, costs about N log N. Barnes and Hut introduced it in 1986.

meanings.short: Boundary conditions that make opposite faces of a box match, so whatever leaves one face, particle or wave, comes back through the other.
meanings.long: Cosmological simulations use a comoving box, typically about 100 megaparsecs across, with periodic boundaries, so there are no edges. In quantum and statistical physics the same trick makes the allowed waves in a box easy to count.

meanings.short: A simulation that re-runs one small region of a larger run at much higher resolution, keeping the rest coarse.
meanings.long: It gives a detailed picture of one galaxy or halo while keeping the pull of its surroundings. Most detailed simulations of single galaxies like the Milky Way are zoom-ins.

meanings.short: A quick model of galaxy formation that takes halos and their merger histories from theory or simulations and adds the gas physics as simple rules.
meanings.long: Semi-analytic models (SAMs) run far faster than full hydrodynamic simulations, so the uncertain recipes for star formation and feedback can be explored widely. Their results are less detailed than full simulations, since galaxies are not resolved in space.

meanings.short: A diagram of how a halo was built: its branches are the smaller halos that merged, step by step, to form it.
meanings.long: Merger trees come from extended Press–Schechter theory or from simulations, and are the backbone of semi-analytic models. The main branch follows the most massive progenitor back in time.

meanings.short: The number of galaxies per unit volume in each range of stellar mass.
meanings.long: It is the most basic test of galaxy-formation models. Its shape, a Schechter-like function, falls below that of the halo mass function at both low and high mass, because feedback limits star formation there.

meanings.short: Linking galaxies to halos by ranking both by mass and pairing them off, so the most massive galaxy goes in the most massive halo.
meanings.long: Matching the observed number of galaxies of each stellar mass to the predicted number of halos gives how much of each halo's share of baryons became stars: at best about a sixth. It assumes that galaxies and halos grow together and that every halo hosts a galaxy.

meanings.short: A statistical rule for how many galaxies, centrals and satellites, live in a halo of a given mass.
meanings.long: Halo occupation distribution (HOD) models use only the halo's mass. A refinement, the conditional luminosity function, also predicts how bright those galaxies are.

meanings.short: The part of galaxy clustering from pairs in the same halo (1-halo term), as opposed to pairs in different halos (2-halo term).
meanings.long: On small scales the correlation function is dominated by the 1-halo term, set by the physics of galaxies; on large scales by the 2-halo term, set by the clustering of halos themselves. The switch between them happens at about the size of large halos, roughly a megaparsec.

meanings.short: A group of galaxies dominated by one giant elliptical, whose other big galaxies have long since merged into it.
meanings.long: Fossil groups formed early and assembled differently from ordinary groups of the same mass, an example of assembly bias. Their X-ray gas shows they are as massive as ordinary groups.

meanings.short: Gravitational lensing that bends light enough to make arcs, rings or several images of one background object.
meanings.long: It happens when the source lies within about an Einstein radius of the lens centre, which needs a surface density near the critical one, usually a massive galaxy or cluster. The positions and shapes of the images weigh the lens very precisely.

meanings.short: Gravitational lensing that only slightly stretches the shapes of background galaxies, measured by averaging over very many of them.
meanings.long: Each galaxy's own shape is unknown, so the tiny shared stretch, the shear, shows only statistically. It maps the mass of clusters and the outer parts of galaxies, dark matter included.

meanings.short: Lensing by an object of about a star's mass, whose images are too close to separate, seen as a background star brightening and fading.
meanings.long: The brightening is symmetric in time, the same in every colour and happens only once. Surveys of millions of stars in the 1990s used it to look for MACHOs in the Milky Way's halo.

meanings.short: A ring of light formed when a background source lies exactly behind a lens, so its image is bent equally all round.
meanings.long: Its angular radius is the Einstein radius. If the alignment is not exact, the ring breaks into arcs or separate images.

meanings.short: The angular radius of the ring a lens would make of a source exactly behind it; it sets the scale of lensing by that lens.
meanings.long: It grows as the square root of the lens mass. For a galaxy it is about an arcsecond; within about one Einstein radius lensing is strong.

meanings.short: The equation linking a background source's true position on the sky to the positions of its lensed images.
meanings.long: It says the image position equals the source position plus the deflection, scaled by a ratio of angular-diameter distances. It can have several solutions: several images.

meanings.short: A scaled, flattened version of a lens's gravitational potential, added up along the line of sight, from which all lensing effects follow.
meanings.long: Its gradient gives the deflection; its second derivatives give the convergence and the shear. It plays the part for lensing that the gravitational potential plays for motion.

meanings.short: In lensing, the lens's surface density divided by the critical surface density; it measures how much images are enlarged evenly.
meanings.long: Written κ. Where κ is near one or more, lensing is strong; weak lensing has κ much less than one.

meanings.short: In lensing, the stretching of an image in one direction and squeezing in the other, which turns round galaxies into slight ellipses.
meanings.long: It has two components, γ₁ and γ₂. Averaged over many background galaxies it maps the mass of the lens, as in the method of Kaiser and Squires.

meanings.short: How many times larger, and so brighter, an image is than the source would look without the lens.
meanings.long: Lensing keeps surface brightness the same, so the brightening equals the ratio of image area to source area. Near a caustic the magnification becomes very large.

origin: Greek kaustikos, burning, from the bright curves of focused light.

meanings.short: A curve behind a lens where the number of images of a source changes and the magnification becomes very large.
meanings.long: The bright curves of light on the bottom of a swimming pool are caustics too. For a circular lens the caustic shrinks to a point.

origin: Greek a-, not, and chroma, colour.

meanings.short: The same for every colour, or wavelength, of light.
meanings.long: Gravity bends all wavelengths equally, so microlensing brightens a star in every colour at once, unlike most variable stars, whose colour changes. Lenses made of glass are not, because glass bends colours differently.

meanings.short: Massive astrophysical compact halo object: a dim body such as a brown dwarf or dead star, once proposed as the dark matter of our halo.
meanings.long: Microlensing surveys of the 1990s, among them the MACHO collaboration, found too few such events: MACHOs make up at most a minor part of the halo. Brown dwarfs, white dwarfs, neutron stars and black holes were all candidates.

meanings.short: A black hole that would have formed in the very early universe, from dense regions rather than from dying stars.
meanings.long: They could have almost any mass and are a proposed dark matter candidate. Microlensing, the cosmic microwave background and gravitational waves limit how much of the dark matter they can be.

everyday: Nothing to do with planets: the name comes from their round look in early telescopes.

meanings.short: A glowing shell of gas thrown off by a dying Sun-like star, lit by the hot core left behind.
meanings.long: Its bright, narrow emission lines can be seen far out in galaxies, so their speeds trace the mass in regions with few other tracers. It lasts only a few tens of thousands of years before fading.

meanings.short: A star late in its life that has swollen to many times its former size and cooled at the surface, so it glows red.
meanings.long: Red giants dominate the light of old stellar populations. Their long lives limit how much energy axions could carry away from stars.

meanings.short: Spreading the light along a narrow slit across a galaxy into a spectrum at every point of the slit.
meanings.long: The Doppler shift of a line at each point gives the speed along that cut: for a rotating disc, an S shape that traces the rotation curve. It gives one cut through a galaxy at a time.

meanings.short: An instrument that takes a spectrum at every point of an image at once, giving a map of speeds across a galaxy.
meanings.long: It shows the full pattern of rotation, including twists and disturbances, which a single slit would miss. Large surveys use them to map the motions of thousands of galaxies.

meanings.short: Combined as the square root of the sum of squares, as the sides of a right-angled triangle give its long side.
meanings.long: Circular speeds from separate parts of a galaxy add this way: v² is the sum of the squares from the stars, the gas and the halo. Independent uncertainties combine in quadrature too.

meanings.short: The tight link between a disc galaxy's total ordinary mass, stars plus gas, and its flat rotation speed: mass grows as speed to the fourth.
meanings.long: Found by Stacy McGaugh and collaborators in 2000. It holds over a huge range of mass and is a key test for both dark matter models and MOND, which predicts it.

meanings.short: The finding that, across many galaxies, the observed acceleration at each radius depends only on the acceleration expected from visible matter.
meanings.long: At large accelerations the two are equal; below about 10⁻¹⁰ m/s² the observed one is larger, all along one tight curve. MOND predicts this; dark matter models must explain why it is so tight.

meanings.short: In MOND, the function that joins Newton's law at large accelerations smoothly to the modified law at small ones.
meanings.long: It tends to one at high accelerations and to the acceleration divided by a₀ at low ones. Its exact form is not fixed by the theory.

meanings.short: A form of MOND as a proper field theory, proposed by Bekenstein and Milgrom in 1984; the name stands for 'a-quadratic Lagrangian'.
meanings.long: It changes the equation for the gravitational potential so that MOND follows, while conserving energy, momentum and angular momentum. It is still not relativistic, so it says nothing about lensing or cosmology.

meanings.short: Tensor–vector–scalar gravity: Bekenstein's 2004 relativistic version of MOND, using three fields.
meanings.long: It was meant to make MOND work for lensing and cosmology. The 2017 observation that gravitational waves travel at the speed of light rules out its original form. Its extra fields make it far more complicated than general relativity.

meanings.short: A proposal that gravity is not a basic force but arises from deeper microscopic physics, in some versions mimicking dark matter.
meanings.long: Verlinde's version links extra gravity in galaxies to dark energy. It remains speculative and is tested against the same data as MOND. Critics argue that it fails to match the dynamics of galaxy clusters.

meanings.short: A proposed kind of neutrino that does not feel the weak force, only gravity, which could be dark matter if it has mass.
meanings.long: The Standard Model has no right-handed neutrinos; an extension can add them, with no weak charge, hence sterile. With a mass of a few keV they would be warm dark matter.

meanings.short: The sea of neutrinos left from the first second after the Big Bang, still filling the universe, now about 1.9 kelvin.
meanings.long: Neutrinos stopped interacting about a second after the Big Bang and have streamed freely since. They are somewhat colder than the microwave background (1.95 K against 2.73 K) because electron–positron annihilation later heated only the photons.

origin: Greek barys, heavy, and genesis, origin.

meanings.short: The unknown process in the early universe that made slightly more matter than antimatter, so that some matter survived.
meanings.long: About one extra baryon per billion pairs was enough. It requires baryon number not to be conserved, and a difference between matter and antimatter (CP violation), among other conditions.

meanings.short: The symmetry under swapping particles for antiparticles (C) and mirror-reflecting space (P) together.
meanings.long: The weak force breaks it slightly. The strong force could break it too, but measurements show it does not, a puzzle that the axion was invented to solve.

meanings.short: A very light proposed particle, invented to explain why the strong force respects CP symmetry, and a leading dark matter candidate.
meanings.long: Peccei and Quinn's mechanism (1977) turns the strong force's CP-violating parameter into a field, whose particle is the axion. Made non-thermally in the early universe, axions would be cold dark matter despite their tiny mass.

meanings.short: A massless particle that appears whenever a continuous symmetry is broken spontaneously; if the symmetry was only approximate, it has a small mass.
meanings.long: Such slightly massive particles are pseudo-Nambu–Goldstone bosons; the pion and the axion are examples. Yoichiro Nambu and Jeffrey Goldstone described them around 1960.

meanings.short: A neutral particle predicted by supersymmetry, a mixture of the partners of the photon, Z boson and Higgs; a classic WIMP candidate.
meanings.long: If it is the lightest supersymmetric particle it is stable. The Large Hadron Collider has so far found no superpartners, which weakens the case.

meanings.short: The lightest of the partner particles predicted by supersymmetry, which would be stable and so a dark matter candidate.
meanings.long: If R-parity is conserved, superpartners can only decay into lighter superpartners, so the lightest one cannot decay at all. The neutralino is the favourite candidate.

meanings.short: A quantity in supersymmetric theories, +1 for ordinary particles and −1 for superpartners, which if conserved makes the lightest superpartner stable.
meanings.long: Its conservation also forbids a superpartner from decaying into ordinary particles alone, and protects the proton from fast decay. Some supersymmetric models break it, in which case the lightest superpartner decays.

meanings.short: The partner particle that supersymmetry gives every known particle, with spin differing by one half.
meanings.long: Fermions get boson partners (squarks, sleptons) and bosons get fermion partners (gluinos, neutralinos, charginos). None has been found.

meanings.short: The point that a lighter particle with a weaker interaction can freeze out with the same dark matter density, escaping detection.
meanings.long: The relic density fixes only a combination of mass and coupling, roughly their ratio, not each separately, so the electroweak scale is not the only possibility. Such particles would escape the searches designed around WIMPs.

meanings.short: An axion detector: a tuned resonant cavity in a strong magnet, in which dark matter axions from the halo would turn into faint microwaves.
meanings.long: The cavity is tuned through possible axion masses one step at a time, and the tiny signal is read out with quantum-limited amplifiers. Several such experiments are running.

meanings.short: Searching for dark matter particles by the tiny recoil of an atomic nucleus they hit in a detector; indirect detection looks for their annihilation products.
meanings.long: Direct detectors are huge, very quiet and deep underground. Indirect searches look for gamma rays, neutrinos or antimatter from places where dark matter is dense; a third way is to make the particles in a collider.

meanings.short: Of a dark matter particle's scattering off a nucleus: not depending on (spin-independent) or depending on (spin-dependent) the nucleus's spin.
meanings.long: The spin-independent part adds up coherently over all nucleons, growing as the square of the mass number, so heavy target nuclei help. Spin-dependent scattering instead depends on the nucleus's unpaired protons or neutrons.

meanings.short: A yearly swing in the rate of dark matter hits, as Earth's orbit adds to or subtracts from the Sun's motion through the halo.
meanings.long: The rate should peak in early June. The DAMA/LIBRA experiment reports such a signal, but other experiments with the same technique do not confirm it.

meanings.short: A small flash of light given off by some materials when a particle deposits energy in them.
meanings.long: Liquid xenon and sodium iodide crystals scintillate, so dark matter detectors count the flashes from nuclear recoils. A material that does this is called a scintillator.

meanings.short: The level below which dark matter detectors cannot easily go, because neutrinos from the Sun and elsewhere make the same kind of recoils.
meanings.long: Neutrinos scattering coherently off nuclei mimic a dark matter signal. It is the ultimate limit of the direct-detection technique.

meanings.short: A ground-based telescope that sees the faint blue flash from showers of particles made when very energetic gamma rays hit the atmosphere.
meanings.long: The flash is Cherenkov light, given off by particles moving faster than light does in air. Such telescopes search for gamma rays from dark matter annihilation.

meanings.short: Energy that seems to vanish in a particle collision, the sign that an unseen particle, such as dark matter or a neutrino, carried it away.
meanings.long: Collider searches for dark matter look for collisions whose visible products are unbalanced in momentum.

meanings.short: The total energy an object gives off as light each second: its true power, whatever its distance.
meanings.long: The Sun's luminosity is about 3.8 × 10²⁶ watts. The flux we receive is the luminosity divided by 4π times the distance squared (in an expanding universe, the luminosity distance).

meanings.short: In a particle collider, the rate of collisions per unit cross-section: how many collisions the beams provide.
meanings.long: Multiplying it by the cross-section of a process gives the rate at which that process happens. It is a property of the beams, not of the particles studied.

origin: Greek polys, many, and tropos, turn.

meanings.short: A model gas whose pressure is a fixed power of its density, used to model stars, compact objects and dark matter halos.
meanings.long: Its equation of state is P = K ρ^(1 + 1/n), with index n. An isothermal gas is the limit of very large n. Its structure follows from the Lane–Emden equation.

meanings.short: The equation for the structure of a self-gravitating ball of polytropic gas in hydrostatic equilibrium.
meanings.long: It combines hydrostatic equilibrium with Poisson's equation, written in dimensionless variables. Only a few indices have solutions in closed form.

meanings.short: Dark matter made of extremely light particles, whose quantum wave nature smooths out structure on scales of about a kiloparsec.
meanings.long: With masses around 10⁻²² eV their wavelengths are galaxy-sized, which would give halos flat cores and suppress the smallest halos. The Lyman-α forest sets lower limits on its particle mass.

meanings.short: A dark matter halo that holds few or no stars, so it can be found only by its gravity.
meanings.long: Cold dark matter predicts many small halos; if star formation was suppressed in most of them, they would be dark galaxies. None has been confirmed so far.

meanings.short: The whole process by which gas falls into dark matter halos, cools, forms stars and becomes the galaxies we see.
meanings.long: It involves gravity, gas physics, star formation and feedback on scales from parsecs to megaparsecs, so it is studied with simulations and simplified models. Its biggest uncertainties are star formation and feedback.

meanings.short: How strong the ripples in the density of matter are on each length scale, written P(k).
meanings.long: Its shape on small scales tells cold from warm or hot dark matter: hot and warm dark matter remove power below their free-streaming length.

meanings.short: A steady state of a system of stars or galaxies in which the distribution of their positions and speeds no longer changes.
meanings.long: For galaxies in a cluster it plays the part that hydrostatic equilibrium plays for the gas, and lets the cluster be weighed with the Jeans equations.

meanings.short: Computing gravity in a simulation by adding up the pull of every particle on every other: exact but slow, about N² steps.
meanings.long: For a billion particles that is far too many operations per step, which is why tree codes and particle–mesh codes were invented. Special hardware such as the GRAPE computers sped it up.

meanings.short: Computing gravity in a simulation by spreading the particles' mass onto a grid and solving for the potential there.
meanings.long: The potential is found with fast Fourier transforms, which is quick, but forces on scales smaller than a grid cell are lost. Hybrid codes add direct sums or a tree for short distances.

origin: Greek helios, sun, and skopein, to look.

meanings.short: An axion detector: a strong magnet pointed at the Sun, in which axions made in the Sun's core would turn into X-rays.
meanings.long: It looks for axions made in the Sun rather than dark matter axions from the halo. Stars losing energy to axions would also live shorter lives, which sets further limits.

meanings.short: A very light particle like the axion that arises in other theories, without the axion's link to the strong force; also a dark matter candidate.
meanings.long: Their masses and couplings are not tied together as for the QCD axion, so experiments search a wide range of both. Made thermally they would be hot relics; made non-thermally they could be cold dark matter.
